title: Baron’s first sense grounds the rest — yet omits the refuge-fiducia of Ames and Wittich
source_text: LIX. Quibus subjungit fiduciam primo modo acceptam esse basin & fundamentum trium sequentium. Quia enim, inquit, firma persuasione, & certo judicio mentis evangelicas promissiones nobis ipsis applicamus, ideo in Dei benevolentia & misericordia acquiescimus; ideo contra mundum, satanam, & carnem nostram fortiter praeliamur; ideo denique conscientiam tranquillam & serenam habemus. Unde patet quod quamvis plures notiones fiduciae proponat, illum tamen omittere, aut non satis attingere, & recte explicare, fiduciam illam perfugii, quae juxta authores supra memoratos, est proprius & formalis actus fidei justificantis. Quippe per eam non acquiescimus in divina gratia & misericordia, quasi jam ejus simus participes; sed ad hoc ut ejus participes fiamus, ad Christum confugimus, & illi innitimur, eoque adhaeremus. Deinde fiducia ista, nascitur quidem ex firmo & solido assensu quem promissionibus Evangelicis adhibemus; sed tamen praecedit assensum specialem, quo bona promissa ad nos pertinere, & nostra jam esse judicamus, ut patet ex iis quae supra relata sunt. Cum contra Baronius velit tres posteriores fiduciae species nasci ex prima, quae ex ejus mente, est ille ipse specialis assensus, quo statuimus Deum nobis omnia nostra peccata remisisse, nosque propter Christum esse in gratiam receptos. Ac praeterea per secundam, juxta Baronium, fiduciae speciem, quae proxime ad descriptam fiduciam accedit, acquiescimus in Dei gratia & misericordia, tanquam de ea jam certo persuasi; non vero simpliciter ad Christum confugimus ut eam consequamur; quod proprium est fiduciae illius, quae verbis Amesii, Wittichii, & Petri Molinaei prolixe fuit a nobis exposita.
pass_a_gloss: To which he subjoins that trust taken in the first way is the base and foundation of the three following. For because, he says, by a firm persuasion and sure judgment of the mind we apply the evangelical promises to our very selves, therefore we rest in God's benevolence and mercy; therefore we fight stoutly against the world, Satan, and our flesh; therefore finally we have a tranquil and serene conscience. Whence it is plain that although he proposes several notions of trust, he nevertheless omits, or does not sufficiently touch and rightly explain, that trust of refuge which according to the authors mentioned above is the proper and formal act of justifying faith. For by it we do not rest in the divine grace and mercy as if we were already partakers of it; but in order that we may become partakers of it we flee to Christ, and lean on Him, and adhere to Him. Then that trust is indeed born from the firm and solid assent which we give to the Evangelical promises; yet it precedes the special assent by which we judge the promised goods to pertain to us and already to be ours, as is plain from what was related above. Whereas on the contrary Baron will have the three later species of trust born from the first, which on his mind is that very special assent by which we lay down that God has remitted all our sins to us, and that for Christ we have been received into grace. And besides, by the second species of trust according to Baron, which comes nearest to the trust described, we rest in God's grace and mercy as already certainly persuaded of it; but we do not simply flee to Christ that we may obtain it — which is proper to that trust which was set forth by us at length in the words of Ames, Wittich, and Peter du Moulin.
pass_b_english: Baron: first-sense fiducia (apply promises) founds rest, fortitude, and peace.
Le Blanc: he still misses refuge-fiducia — flee/lean on Christ to become a partaker, not rest as already one.
Refuge-fiducia is born from solid Gospel assent but precedes special ‘already mine’ assent.
Baron’s first sense = special remitted-assent; his second = rest as already persuaded — not simple fleeing to obtain.
